Stage 3 · Reading

Sixty days without a sunrise

Two months of polar night at 69° north — and the research on why it is not what visitors expect.

🌑❄️
1 · Before you read. Two months without a sunrise. What would you expect the effect on people to be?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

Sixty days without a sunrise

Written for this course, from Johnsen, Wynn & Bratlid, BMC Psychiatry 12:225 (2012), and Leibowitz & Vittersø’s work on wintertime mindset at the University of Tromsø.

1The first thing anybody asks, once they hear where I live, is how I cope with the dark. Tromsø sits at just over sixty-nine degrees north, well above the Arctic Circle, and for about two months the sun never climbs above the horizon at all. People automatically assume that those weeks must be miserable. They are not. They are the part of the year I would keep if somebody made me choose.

2The cause is not the weather but the tilt of the Earth’s axis, which is basically twenty-three and a half degrees and which everybody learns at school and nobody believes until they have lived through it. Above a certain line the polar night simply arrives. During the darkest weeks the town gets two or three hours of indirect light, thrown up into the sky from a sun that is still below the ridge. The sky turns deep blue late in the morning, grows slightly lighter for an hour, and then closes again. Winters in my homeland are considerably shorter and dramatic in a different way: bitterly cold, brutally bright, and finished by March.

3What surprises visitors most is how rarely anybody stays indoors. Children are outside at nine in the morning, dressed extremely warmly, playing under artificial light on the school field. The ski track on the mountainside above the town is lit from end to end, and it is used far more heavily in December than in April. Houses are lit softly too, with a candle in almost every window, which sounds sentimental and is basically practical: it makes a street feel cosy rather than closed.

4The research is more interesting than the postcard. A large population study published in 2012, covering nearly nine thousand adults in Tromsø, found no significant seasonal difference in mental distress at all — but it did find that sleeping problems were significantly more common in winter than in any other season. That is a careful result rather than a cheerful one. The darkness appears to cost people their sleep without costing them their mood, which is not the story either the optimists or the pessimists usually tell.

5Why the mood holds up is a separate question, and one answer points at expectation. A health psychologist who spent ten months in the town, working with a colleague at the university there, built a short questionnaire measuring whether residents saw winter as something to be enjoyed or something to be endured. People who scored highly on it — who agreed that there was a great deal to enjoy in the season — reported greater life satisfaction and more positive emotion. The contrast with how the same months are described further south is striking, and it is cultural before it is biological.

6Then, gradually, it comes back. On the morning the sun first appears above the ridge, the whole town behaves slightly oddly and extremely happily; people stand on the harbour wall and watch for the twenty minutes it lasts. Six months later the opposite arrives, and it is not automatically easier. By June it never really gets dark, which is magical for a week and mildly irritating for the two months afterwards.

Text A · What two months of night are actually like

Written for this course.

The first thing anybody asks, once they hear where I live, is how I cope with the dark. Tromsø sits at just over sixty-nine degrees north, well above the Arctic Circle, and for about two months the sun never climbs above the horizon at all. People automatically assume that those weeks must be miserable. They are not. They are the part of the year I would keep if somebody made me choose.

The cause is not the weather but the tilt of the Earth’s axis, which is basically twenty-three and a half degrees and which everybody learns at school and nobody believes until they have lived through it. Above a certain line the polar night simply arrives. During the darkest weeks the town gets two or three hours of indirect light, thrown up into the sky from a sun that is still below the ridge. The sky turns deep blue late in the morning, grows slightly lighter for an hour, and then closes again. What surprises visitors most is how rarely anybody stays indoors. Children are outside at nine in the morning, dressed extremely warmly, playing under artificial light on the school field. Houses are lit softly too, with a candle in almost every window, which sounds sentimental and is basically practical: it makes a street feel cosy rather than closed.

Text B · What the research says about it

Written for this course, from Johnsen, Wynn & Bratlid, BMC Psychiatry 12:225 (2012), and Leibowitz & Vittersø’s work on wintertime mindset at the University of Tromsø.

The research is more interesting than the postcard. A large population study published in 2012, covering nearly nine thousand adults in Tromsø, found no significant seasonal difference in mental distress at all — but it did find that sleeping problems were significantly more common in winter than in any other season. That is a careful result rather than a cheerful one. The darkness appears to cost people their sleep without costing them their mood, which is not the story either the optimists or the pessimists usually tell.

Why the mood holds up is a separate question, and one answer points at expectation. A health psychologist who spent ten months in the town, working with a colleague at the university there, built a short questionnaire measuring whether residents saw winter as something to be enjoyed or something to be endured. People who scored highly on it — who agreed that there was a great deal to enjoy in the season — reported greater life satisfaction and more positive emotion. The contrast with how the same months are described further south is striking, and it is cultural before it is biological.

Then, gradually, it comes back. On the morning the sun first appears above the ridge, the whole town behaves slightly oddly and extremely happily; people stand on the harbour wall and watch for the twenty minutes it lasts. Six months later the opposite arrives, and it is not automatically easier. By June it never really gets dark, which is magical for a week and mildly irritating for the two months afterwards. Nobody who has not lived through both seasons quite believes that the light one can be the harder of the two.

1 · Read the explanation.
What the word is describing

An adjective describes a noun: a dramatic change, the polar night. An adverb describes a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence: it changed dramatically, considerably colder, extremely warmly, basically, the plan works. Almost every error at this level comes from answering that first question wrongly rather than from not knowing the ending.

Forming them. Most adverbs are the adjective plus -ly. Adjectives in -y change to -ily (happy → happily); adjectives in -ic add -ally (dramatic → dramatically, automatic → automatically, basic → basically); adjectives in -le drop the e (gentle → gently). Some adverbs have no -ly: fast, hard, early, late, straight, and the irregular good → well.

The trap. A word ending in -ly is not automatically an adverb. Friendly, lively, lonely, silly and likely are adjectives with no adverb form at all, so English says she spoke to me in a friendly way. And three pairs mean quite different things: hard (with effort) against hardly (almost not), late (not on time) against lately (recently), near (close) against nearly (almost).

After a linking verb, use an adjective. Be, feel, look, seem, sound, taste, smell and become describe the subject, not the action: it feels cosy, it looks magical, the plan sounds dramatic. Compare she looked cold (that was her state) with she looked coldly at him (that was the way she looked at him).

Position and degree
  • Manner adverbs go after the verb, or after the object: she speaks Norwegian well.
  • Degree adverbs go immediately before the word they modify: slightly darker, extremely warmly.
  • Comment adverbs go at the front or in mid position: Basically, it works · people automatically assume.
  • Before comparatives use slightly, considerably, far, much, a lot — never very: far colder, not very colder.

Two things to watch

1 — Very cannot stand in front of a comparative. Very colder is impossible; use much, far, a lot, considerably or slightly instead. Very is only for the base form: very cold.

2 — Good is never an adverb. She speaks English good is one of the most noticeable errors at any level: it is speaks English well. Note that well is also an adjective meaning “not ill”, which is why I feel well and I feel good both exist and mean slightly different things.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Two questions decide everything

First: what is the word describing? A noun takes an adjective (a dramatic change, the polar night); a verb, an adjective or another adverb takes an adverb (the light comes back gradually, considerably colder, dressed extremely warmly).

Second, if it is an adverb, how is it formed? -ly in most cases (soft → softly); -y becomes -ily (happy → happily, easy → easily); -ic gains an extra al (dramatic → dramatically); -le drops the e (gentle → gently, possible → possibly); and a handful are irregular or unchanged: good → well, fast, hard, early, late.

The trap is the group that ends in -ly and is not an adverb at all: friendly, lively, lonely, likely, silly, ugly. There is no friendlily; you say they treated us in a friendly way.

Linking verbs, position, and the pairs that change meaning

After linking verbs — be, seem, look, feel, sound, taste, smell, become, get — the word describes the subject, so it is an adjective: It feels cosy, The plan sounds dramatic. It feels cosily is wrong. Compare She looked angry (that is how she seemed) with She looked at me angrily (that is how she did it).

Position: adverbs of manner normally follow the verb or its object (He closed the door gently); degree adverbs go in front of the adjective or adverb they modify (considerably shorter); frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be (She always arrives early · She is always late).

Finally the pairs where the -ly form means something else entirely: hard (with effort) against hardly (almost not) · late against lately (recently) · near against nearly (almost). She works hard and She hardly works are opposites.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a piece for the series

The two months nobody believes me about are January and July, and the contrast between them is considerably larger than any photograph makes it look. In January the temperature stays around minus twenty for weeks, the wind arrives from the steppe with nothing in its way, and the light is thin and grey by three in the afternoon. In July the same street is thirty-five degrees at four o’clock and completely empty.

What visitors automatically assume is that everybody hides indoors from November to March. They do not. The skating rink in the park is busiest at seven in the evening in the dark, children are walked to school in temperatures that would close a school in western Europe, and the buses run exactly as usual. People simply dress for it, extremely seriously, and treat anybody who does not as slightly foolish.

The change between the two happens surprisingly fast. April does most of it in about ten days: the snow goes dirty, then grey, then gone, and the city smells of wet earth for a fortnight. It does not arrive gradually the way spring does further west.

And, honestly, the summer I am supposed to prefer is the part I like least. It looks magical in photographs and it feels airless by the middle of the afternoon. If I had to keep one month, I would keep the cold one, which surprises everybody except the people who live here.
